items.title: CVE-2026-102895: GPUStack Improper Authentication Vulnerability
items.detail: GPUStack contains an improper authentication vulnerability which could allow unauthenticated administrative access, including user and model changes, persistent administrator API-key creation, disclosure of worker and cloud-provider secrets, and code execution through POST /v2/inference-backends/from-yaml. Required action: Apply mitigations in accordance with vendor instructions, ensuring compliance with CISA’s BOD 26-04 Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk (see URL in Notes) guidance and CISA’s “Forensics Triage Requirements” (see URL in Notes). Follow applicable BOD 26-04 guidance for cloud services or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable. Stakeholders are responsible for evaluating each asset's internet exposure and ensuring adherence to BOD 26-04 patching guidelines. Catalog addition date is not the attack date.

items.title: FORGE Lab uses agentic tools to identify memory safety issues in Rust
items.detail: In this article How we found and validated the bugs Pattern 1: Trusting code not to panic Pattern 2: Trusting user-provided implementations to be correct Pattern 3: Trusting the underlying system Why Rust still matters and advancing vulnerability discovery with AI Rust's high bar is hard to meet but worth keeping Microsoft’s FORGE Lab found several memory safety issues in Rust’s standard library (std and core), including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. The research used Hyenas, FORGE’s frontier research version of codename MDASH, an AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system. The findings reveal three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system. Rust’s safety guarantees are precisely what make these findings interesting. Its rich type system and ownership model rule out whole classes of memory-safety issues, but much of the standard library relies on unsafe code underneath its safe APIs. When that code breaks its safety contract, even safe Rust can encounter behavior the language is designed to prevent. Rust’s memory-safety guarantees are increasingly important as the language becomes part of software that billions of people rely on every day. Billions of people are estimated to interact with Rust-based software or operating systems daily, often without knowing it. Microsoft made Rust a Tier-1 internal language alongside C++, C#, and TypeScript, GitHub rewrote the Copilot agent runtime in Rust , and Bun , Android , the Linux kernel , and Cloudflare are moving code to it as well. Much of this software relies on Rust’s foundational libraries, core and std, and the safety guarantees of the APIs they provide. Bugs in those libraries can have consequences well beyond the code where they originate. Unsafe Rust has been a long-running interest for us. Our team includes the people behind Rudra , a static analyzer that looked for memory-safety bugs across the Rust ecosystem in 2021. We also write many of our own tools in Rust, so its safety is more than a research topic for us. This year, we took a closer look at the standard library to see what kinds of mistakes still show up in its unsafe code today. In this post, we share some of the bugs we reported to the Rust issue tracker. We use them to discuss what Rust does and doesn’t guarantee, why writing correct unsafe Rust is so difficult, and why Rust’s safety model still matters even though its memory safety isn’t perfect. How we found and validated the bugs At Microsoft FORGE Lab , we study vulnerabilities in complex software, including the Rust standard library. Our team combines years of experience in vulnerability research with AI-assisted tools that help us investigate code and find bugs that are difficult to uncover through traditional analysis alone. Some of the bugs in this post were found with help from Hyenas, our research version of codename MDASH. Our researchers investigated the underlying code, reproduced the bugs, assessed their potential security impact, and worked with Rust maintainers to report and fix them. This post focuses on soundness bugs in the standard library’s unsafe code. Bugs in the compiler itself, such as miscompilations and holes in the type system, are a different topic that we don’t cover here. A note on open issues At publication, two of the issues reported by our team remain open. The article also references related issues reported by others and fixes that are still under review. The Rust maintainers triaged and responded to our reports quickly, and we believe maintainers and the contributors working on these issues are doing their best and making the right tradeoffs among the many bugs they handle. If you’re interested in an open issue, please comment only when you have something genuinely new to contribute, such as new information or an affected real-world use case. Patterns of Rust’s Safety Bugs At the lowest level, Rust uses unsafe blocks to work with raw pointers and interact directly with the operating system. Much of the standard library, including Vec and String, is built from small unsafe pieces wrapped in safe APIs. Inside an unsafe block, the programmer takes responsibility for the guarantees the compiler can’t check, and that responsibility extends to the safe API built around it. That API must be sound : no matter how safe code uses it, it must be impossible to trigger undefined behavior. Upholding that promise is harder than it looks. Consider a function that returns the byte at idx from any type that can be viewed as a byte slice, skipping the redundant bounds check after doing its own: pub fn get < ​S: AsRef < ​[u8]>>(s: &S, idx: usize) -> Option < ​u8> { if idx < s.as_ref().len() { Some(unsafe { *s.as_ref().get_unchecked(idx) }) } else { None } } The hard part of unsafe Rust is knowing what you can trust. The function above looks correct, but it assumes that two calls to as_ref return the same slice. Because S is chosen by the caller, a safe AsRef implementation can return a long slice the first time and an empty one the second, and get reads out of bounds. Unsafe code must be careful with every call it makes, and the bugs we found fall into three patterns of misplaced trust: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system. Pattern 1: Trusting code not to panic Unsafe code often breaks an invariant for a moment and restores it afterward; for example, it may allocate an uninitialized buffer and fill it directly, avoiding redundant writes to zero the memory first. That’s fine as long as the function runs to the end. But many operations in Rust can panic, from out-of-bounds indexing to calls into user-provided code, and by default a panic unwinds: it leaves the function early while still running destructors. Unwinding inside that window becomes an invisible exit that exposes the broken invariant to code that trusts it. Bugs of this kind are called panic safety bugs. Figure 1 — Panic Safety. MapWindows::clone (issue #156501) We identified a panic safety issue in MapWindows::clone . The nightly API Iterator::map_windows yields overlapping windows of N items. It keeps the current window in a Buffer whose destructor drops the N items starting at start . In Rust 1.97.0, library/core/src/iter/adapters/map_windows.rs defines it as: struct Buffer < ​T, const N: usize> { // Invariant: `self.buffer[self.start..self.start + N]` is initialized, // with all other elements being uninitialized. This also // implies that `self.start < = N`. buffer: [[MaybeUninit < ​T>; N]; 2], start: usize, } Buffer::clone , in the same file, built the new buffer first and filled it afterward: impl < ​T: Clone, const N: usize> Clone for Buffer < ​T, N> { fn clone(&self) -> Self { let mut buffer = Buffer { buffer: [[const { MaybeUninit::uninit() }; N], [const { MaybeUninit::uninit() }; N]], start: self.start, }; buffer.as_uninit_array_mut().write(self.as_array_ref().clone()); buffer } } After buffer is constructed , it breaks its own invariant: its slots are uninitialized, but its destructor is already armed. The self.as_array_ref().clone() call runs the user's T::clone before the slots are written. If that call panics, unwinding drops buffer and runs drop_in_place on N uninitialized values. Our proof of concept uses only safe code: an element type whose clone always panics, which causes a crash when the destructor accesses uninitialized memory. The fix holds the new buffer in ManuallyDrop until it is fully written, so unwinding leaks the half-built buffer instead of dropping it. The general lesson is to treat every call to code you don’t control, such as clone, drop, comparisons, closures, and iterator methods, as a possible early exit. Either finish the work that may panic before breaking an invariant, or make the broken state safe to unwind through: hold it in ManuallyDrop, or use a guard whose destructor restores the invariant, like Vec’s internal SetLenOnDrop. The Rustonomicon covers this under exception safety . Allocators must not unwind The recently stabilized Allocator API shows how hard panic safety is to get right. With std, an allocation failure aborts the process by default instead of unwinding, so much of the standard library's unsafe code assumes allocation never unwinds. Custom allocators can break that assumption. While the API was being stabilized, we reported one place in BTreeMap::insert that becomes unsound when an allocator unwinds, and others reported more ( #159334 , #159368 , #159370 ). Fixing them one by one would mean auditing everything that allocates, so the stabilization , shipping in Rust 1.100 on November 12, instead requires implementors never to unwind from the trait's methods or from drop. The proposal notes that "unwinding out of many allocation-related methods was found to be a pervasive source of unsoundness." Pattern 2: Trusting user-provided implementations to be correct Unsafe code often calls into code its caller provides: a comparator, a trait implementation, a closure. That code is safe, but safe doesn’t mean correct, and it can return inconsistent or plainly wrong answers. The question is who is responsible when it does. In C++, it’s the caller. std::sort requires its comparator to be a strict weak ordering, and breaking that rule is undefined behavior. With libstdc++, sorting equal elements with <= reads past the end of the vector: std::vector < ​int> v(100, 42); // Bug: ` < =` is not a strict weak ordering, since cmp(a, a) is true. std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a < = b; }); // AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow in std::__introsort_loop The same comparator passed to Rust's sort_by is only a logic error. The sort may panic or leave the slice in an unspecified order, but it never causes undefined behavior. The responsibility sits with the unsafe code. The comparator is safe code supplied by the caller, so the unsafe code inside the sort must stay sound no matter what it returns. The same goes for every safe trait a user can implement: comparisons can be inconsistent, an ExactSizeIterator can report a length that doesn't match the items it yields, and Borrow can return a different value on each call. str::replace with a custom Pattern (#156491) Another of our bug reports shows how easy this trust is to miss: str::replace with a custom Pattern can create a non-UTF-8 String . String search APIs accept any type that implements the nightly Pattern trait, and a pattern can describe itself through as_utf8_pattern. str::replace uses that description to take a fast path when replacing one ASCII byte with another. In Rust 1.96.0, the fast path in library/alloc/src/str.rs looked like this: pub fn replace < ​P: Pattern>(&self, from: P, to: &str) -> String { // Fast path for replacing a single ASCII character with another. if let Some(from_byte) = match from.as_utf8_pattern() { Some(Utf8Pattern::StringPattern([from_byte])) => Some(*from_byte), Some(Utf8Pattern::CharPattern(c)) => c.as_ascii().map(|ascii_char| ascii_char.to_u8()), _ => None, } { if let [to_byte] = to.as_bytes() { return unsafe { replace_ascii(self.as_bytes(), from_byte, *to_byte) }; } } replace_ascii , in the same file, then rewrites the bytes: unsafe fn replace_ascii(utf8_bytes: &[u8], from: u8, to: u8) -> String { let result: Vec < ​u8> = utf8_bytes.iter().map(|b| if *b == from { to } else { *b }).collect(); // SAFETY: We replaced ascii with ascii on valid utf8 strings. unsafe { String::from_utf8_unchecked(result) } } The CharPattern branch checks that the character is ASCII, but the StringPattern branch assumes a one-byte string pattern must be ASCII. That holds for &str patterns, but StringPattern stored &[u8], and as_utf8_pattern is a safe method any Pattern can implement. In our proof of concept, a custom pattern reports the single byte 0x80, which only appears inside multibyte UTF-8 sequences: impl Pattern for NonAsciiBytePattern { // ... fn as_utf8_pattern(&self) -> Option < ​Utf8Pattern < ​'_>> { static NEEDLE: [u8; 1] = [0x80]; Some(Utf8Pattern::StringPattern(&NEEDLE)) } } // "\u{d000}" is [ed, 80, 80]; the result is [ed, 3f, 3f], which is not UTF-8. let corrupted = "\u{d000}".replace(NonAsciiBytePattern, "?"); str::replace rewrites the continuation bytes and returns a String that isn't valid UTF-8, and later string operations that rely on UTF-8 reach undefined behavior. The fix changed StringPattern to hold &str instead of &[u8], so the type itself now guarantees UTF-8. When unsafe code depends on a property of a user-provided implementation, don’t take it on faith. Call the implementation once and keep the result, validate what it returns, or encode the property in a type that safe code can’t forge, as this fix did. If none of those work, make the trait unsafe so implementors explicitly promise to uphold it. More examples join shows how easy it is to fix this kind of bug only partway. In 2020, we reported that it trusted Borrow::borrow to return the same string on each call ( CVE-2020-36323 ), and the fix handled strings that shrink between calls. In April 2026, the same function needed another fix : join borrows the first element twice, and if it grows on the second call, the remaining-length calculation underflows into a heap overflow. The earlier fix had never covered that path. Others reported similar problems in the Pattern API this year. A safe Pattern can hand back a valid searcher built for a different string, and consumers such as strip_prefix_of apply its ranges to the original string unchecked, reading out of bounds ( #158265 ). The same problem turned up in split_once ( #165076 ) after a report that the Searcher contract doesn't spell out what str::split relies on ( #164904 ). Both bugs are still open. Pattern 3: Trusting the underlying system The first two patterns stay inside Rust code. The third sits at the boundary with the operating system, where unsafe code trusts process-wide state such as signal stacks, memory mappings, and the environment, which other threads, C libraries, or the kernel can touch at any time. These bugs have been hard to find automatically, because a static analyzer would need to model all of that surrounding behavior. AI agents change the picture: they understand enough about the environment the code runs in to make this area practical to search. We started exploring it and found some interesting bugs. process::exit and the main thread’s signal stack (#161018) When a thread overflows its stack, Rust prints a clear message and aborts instead of crashing with a bare segmentation fault: thread 'main' (3307186) has overflowed its stack fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting This relies on a few pieces of process-wide state. Each thread’s stack ends in a guard page, an inaccessible region just past the stack’s limit: pthread reserves one for every spawned thread, and on Linux the kernel’s own stack guard plays that role for the main thread. Touching it raises SIGSEGV, and Rust registers a handler for that signal. The handler can’t run on the stack that just overflowed, so Rust also gives each thread an alternate signal stack, a small separate mapping with a guard page of its own, which the kernel switches to when it delivers the signal. The handler checks that the faulting address is inside the guard page, prints the message, and aborts. Figure 2 — Stack Overflow. We found that calling process::exit from a child thread tears down the main thread’s alternate stack while the main thread is still running. process::exit runs the runtime’s cleanup before calling libc’s exit, and in Rust 1.98.0 that cleanup ends in library/std/src/sys/pal/unix/stack_overflow.rs : pub unsafe fn cleanup() { if cfg!(panic = "immediate-abort") { return; } // FIXME: I probably cause more bugs than I'm worth! // see https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/111272 unsafe { drop_handler(MAIN_ALTSTACK.load(Ordering::Relaxed)) }; } The cleanup function passes MAIN_ALTSTACK, the main thread’s alternate stack, to drop_handler : // SAFETY: we warned the caller this disables the alternate signal stack! unsafe { sigaltstack(&disabling_stack, ptr::null_mut()) }; // SAFETY: We know from `get_stackp` that the alternate stack we installed is part of // a mapping that started one page earlier, so walk back a page and unmap from there. unsafe { munmap(data.sub(page_size), sigstack_size + page_size) }; The call to sigaltstack disables the alternate stack of the calling thread, but the subsequent call to munmap unmaps the main thread’s. The code assumes it runs on the main thread, which isn’t true when a child thread calls process::exit. The main thread keeps running until libc’s exit finishes, with its signal stack registration still pointing at unmapped memory. If it overflows its stack in that window, the kernel can’t deliver the signal, and our proof of concept dies with a plain segmentation fault instead of Rust’s message. The bug dates back to 2015 , and the fix stops cleaning up the main thread’s alternate stack altogether. We also checked whether this could become a security issue. In theory, it could lead to code execution: if a writable mapping landed at the old alternate stack’s address, the kernel would deliver the main thread’s next signal onto it, and another thread could overwrite the handler’s frame, such as its return address, while it runs. In practice, the conditions are very tight. Everything has to happen in the brief window before libc’s exit finishes, the new mapping must have exactly the right size to reuse that address, and overwriting the frame takes a second race inside a short handler. For issue #161018, our testing found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions examined, and we assessed practical exploitation as unlikely. This assessment does not automatically apply to the other issues discussed. The issue has more details in its security impact analysis. CommandExt::exec and the global environment (#156951) Our other report involves the process environment. On Unix, CommandExt::exec replaces the current process with a new program. When the command has its own environment variables, exec points the process-global environ at a new array, calls execvp, and restores environ if execvp fails. In Rust 1.99.0, Command::exec takes the environment lock in library/std/src/sys/process/unix/unix.rs : let _lock = sys::env::env_read_lock(); let Err(e) = self.do_exec(theirs, envp.as_ref()); Command::do_exec , in the same file, then swaps the environment: _reset = Some(Reset(*sys::env::environ())); *sys::env::environ() = envp.as_ptr(); } libc::execvp(self.get_program_cstr().as_ptr(), self.get_argv().as_ptr()); Err(io::Error::last_os_error()) Command::exec takes only the read side of the environment lock, yet do_exec writes the process-global environ . Before the write, do_exec saves the old value so it can be restored if execvp fails. Writing environ under a read lock lets other threads in. A thread calling env::var takes the same read lock and can see variables meant only for the new program, and two failed exec calls racing each other can leave environ pointing at a freed array that a later env::vars_os() reads. Both proofs of concept use only safe Rust. A 2018 fix held an exclusive lock here, but when the environment lock became a read-write lock in 2021, exec kept the read side. A fix that avoids touching environ by calling execve directly is in review . The environment has caused trouble before. After a discussion that began in 2015 , the 2024 edition marked env::set_var as unsafe , because C functions on most Unix platforms read the environment without going through Rust's lock. process::exit and thread-local destructors (#164243) Getting this boundary right is hard, and more problems are still open. While exploring this area, we independently ran into a double free in safe code that process::exit can cause through thread-local destructors. It was reported by someone else ( #164243 ), but it’s worth mentioning here. libc’s exit first runs the calling thread’s thread-local destructors, as C++ requires, and Rust registers its destructors the same way. If a destructor calls process::exit while a thread local is being replaced, libc drops that thread local a second time. A proposed fix switches process::exit to POSIX _exit, which ends the process without running these handlers. Why Rust still matters and advancing vulnerability discovery with AI Every unsafe block rests on assumptions about the code around it. The bugs in this post came from three kinds of misplaced trust: that code won't panic at the wrong moment, that a caller-provided implementation behaves correctly, and that the process-wide state Rust shares with the operating system and the C library stays the way the code expects. Familiar patterns are still difficult (Patterns 1 and 2) The first two patterns are well studied. Rudra looked for both in 2021, and the standard library was already fixing panic safety bugs in 2015 ( CVE-2015-20001 ). They remain challenging to avoid because any call inside unsafe code might unwind or run code the caller supplied. What we saw this year was mixed. On the positive side, the nightly process is working. Many reports were caught while the affected APIs were still unstable, and several were fixed by changing the design before stabilization. StringPattern now holds &str instead of &[u8] , and Allocator was stabilized with a rule that implementors must not unwind. At the same time, bugs in these patterns still reach stable releases, and their fixes aren't always complete. join was fixed in 2020 and needed another fix in 2026 for a path the first fix had missed. System boundary bugs are now within reach (Pattern 3) The third pattern is different. Its bugs live where Rust meets the layers below it: the kernel, through system calls such as sigaltstack and munmap, and the C library, through process-wide state such as environ and the cleanup that libc's exit runs. Getting them right takes knowledge that lives outside Rust's type system, which has made these bugs difficult to find with traditional static analysis. That may also be why they last so long. The process::exit signal stack bug was in the standard library for nearly 11 years, and exec has written environ under a read lock since 2021. Unlike our reports in the first two patterns, both affect stable Rust. Language models already know a great deal about how these interfaces behave, so agentic scanners can check unsafe code against the system it runs on, not just the language. We think this boundary is one of the most promising places for agentic security research, in Rust and beyond. Rust's high bar is hard to meet but worth keeping Rust holds its safe APIs to a stricter standard than C and C++. Safe code must never be able to cause undefined behavior, no matter how it uses an API. In C++, a comparator that breaks std::sort's ordering requirement causes undefined behavior, while Rust's sort must stay memory-safe with any Ord implementation. POSIX doesn't guarantee that setenv is safe to call while another thread reads the environment. That makes memory safety bugs in Rust hard to compare one-to-one with bugs in other languages. For the same reason, a soundness bug in the standard library isn't automatically a vulnerability in the programs that use it. Each bug in this post needs an unusual setup to trigger, such as a panic at exactly the wrong moment, a deliberately misbehaving implementation, or calling process::exit from a child thread. It becomes a serious vulnerability only if a real program reaches the API in that way. Rust's safety standard is strict and difficult to meet, but it's also useful. It gives an unambiguous answer to what counts as a soundness bug, so problems can be fixed and prevented once in the library, instead of in every program that uses it. Rust's safety model strikes the right balance between control, safety, and performance for systems programming, which is why so many projects choose it. Beyond the lab At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we're exploring how technology such as codename MDASH can help researchers find bugs like the ones in this post at greater scale. Rust's standard library is one of several foundational open source projects where we're applying this approach. This research also extends beyond the lab. It helps inform the development of codename MDASH, which brings agentic vulnerability discovery into Microsoft Defender. These findings can also serve as inputs to Microsoft Perception, our new multi-agent security system, where specialized agents work together across broader security workflows. For example, the Web App Pen Test Agent can use codename MDASH findings to help prioritize testing, validate exploitability against live applications, and produce actionable vulnerabilities that downstream agents can use to prioritize and support remediation. This connects AI-powered code analysis with real-world security validation and response, helping security teams move from identifying potential vulnerabilities to understanding and addressing actual risk. Our goal isn’t to simply find more bugs, it's to identify meaningful issues, turn those findings into actionable research, and improve the safety of foundational software that developers and organizations depend on. The post FORGE Lab uses agentic tools to identify memory safety issues in Rust appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

items.detail: IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Non-mobile statistics IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Mobile statistics The statistics in this report are based on detection verdicts returned by Kaspersky products unless otherwise stated. The information was provided by Kaspersky users who consented to sharing statistical data. Quarterly figures In Q3 2026: Kaspersky products blocked more than 311 million attacks launched from online resources. Web Anti-Virus responded to 47 million unique links. File Anti-Virus blocked more than 23 million malicious and potentially unwanted objects. There were 4470 new ransomware variants discovered. More than 81,000 users experienced ransomware attacks. 15% of all ransomware victims whose data was published on threat actors’ data leak sites (DLSs) were victims of Qilin. More than 217,000 users were targeted by miners. Ransomware Quarterly trends and highlights Threat actor disruption In August, the creator and lead administrator of the Ransom Cartel ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation was sentenced to 16 years in prison. The convict developed the ransomware Trojan and at the time of his arrest played a central role in the RaaS operation: running the affiliate program, recruiting affiliates, supplying them with information and attack tools, working with initial access brokers, communicating with victims, and processing payments. In September, a member of the Ryuk RaaS group was sentenced to two years in prison and three years of supervised release. In 2019 and 2020, he and his accomplices breached organizations’ networks and encrypted data with the Ryuk Trojan. According to public reports, hundreds of workstations and servers were compromised. According to the prosecution, the attacker received a total of about 1610 BTC in ransom payments from victims. Also in September, a member of the Conti RaaS group was sentenced to four years in prison. He was charged with attacking companies in 2021 and 2022. In addition to carrying out attacks, he developed part of the group’s malware toolkit. Vulnerabilities and attacks In July, researchers published a report on the Qilin group exploiting the CVE-2026-0257 vulnerability in Palo Alto Networks firewall software. The vulnerability allowed attackers to bypass authentication and compromise victims’ networks without valid accounts. CISA published information in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog (KEV) on several CVEs actively exploited by ransomware groups: CVE-2026-15409 / CVE-2026-15410 in SonicWall SMA1000 remote access gateways. CISA doesn’t specify which groups exploited these vulnerabilities, but researchers have linked this activity to INC Ransom. CVE-2026-45659 in Microsoft SharePoint Server allowed an authenticated, low-privileged attacker to achieve remote code execution. CVE-2025-60710 in Microsoft Windows allowed attackers to escalate privileges locally. CVE-2026-59310 in VMware vCenter enabled unauthenticated remote code execution. CVE-2025-14733 in WatchGuard Firebox also enabled unauthenticated remote code execution. CVE-2026-63077 in JetBrains TeamCity allowed OS commands to run with the privileges of the TeamCity server process by way of an authentication bypass through the agent polling protocol. Command execution at that level could give access to configurations, credentials, CI/CD pipelines, and more. The most prolific groups This section highlights the most prolific ransomware gangs by number of victims added to each group’s DLS. Qilin (15.39%) holds first place, as it did last quarter. Qilin is followed by The Gentlemen (7.89%), which was especially active in Q1 but did not make the list in Q2. A notable newcomer on the list is Deadlock (4.46%), a relatively young ransomware family first reported in July 2025. Number of new ransomware modifications, Q3 2025 – Q3 2026 ( download ) Number of users attacked by ransomware Trojans During the reporting period, our products protected 81,556 unique users from ransomware attacks. After the spike in the second quarter, it’s fair to say the pattern has returned to the calmer one typical of last year. Attacks on macOS Quarterly highlights At the beginning of the third quarter, Jamf researchers discovered a new stealer, PamStealer. What sets it apart is its use of Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) to verify the administrator password the user enters. During the quarter, Socket researchers discovered several supply chain attacks that compromised popular npm, PyPI and Cargo (the Rust package manager) packages. The malicious payloads in these packages targeted macOS systems along with others. For example, on July 11, an infected npm package, jscrambler, was published . Its malicious module was an infostealer written in Rust. The infostealer targeted crypto wallets, secrets from various services and browsers, MCP server configurations, and API keys for AI agents. In August, an attack was detected on the arrayref, internment, and append-only-vec Rust crates; it delivered a Rust backdoor to the victim’s device. In September, malicious versions of the MemTensor npm and PyPI packages were published . They delivered a Go backdoor that targeted secrets, configurations, and API tokens of various services. In August, Jamf researchers also reported discovering a new backdoor, Overlord . It was distributed as fake Zoom installers and had fairly broad spyware functionality, which is not often seen in macOS backdoors: it could eavesdrop through the microphone, watch the user through the camera, capture the screen, and log keystrokes. In the third quarter, we discovered an updated version of the MacSync crypto stealer and backdoor with a significantly changed payload delivery method. The share of Ngrok, a network tunneling tool suite with both legitimate and malicious uses, continued to grow, bringing it to the top of the list. We’re also seeing more detections of the well-known Amos malware, both the traditional stealer and a version with backdoor functionality. These malicious pages are purposefully created by cybercriminals. Websites that host user-generated content, such as message boards, as well as compromised legitimate sites, can become infected. One or more web-based attacks could originate from each unique host. To determine the geographic source of web attacks, we matched each domain name to the actual IP address hosting it, then geolocated that address (GeoIP). items.title: IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Mobile statistics
items.detail: IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Non-mobile statistics IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Mobile statistics The mobile section of the quarterly cyberthreat report includes statistics on malware, adware, and potentially unwanted software for Android, as well as descriptions of the most notable threats for Android and iOS discovered during the reporting period. These statistics are based on detection alerts from Kaspersky products, collected from users who consented to provide statistical data to Kaspersky Security Network. The quarter in figures According to Kaspersky Security Network, in Q3 2026: More than 1.66 million attacks involving mobile malware, adware, or unwanted software were blocked. The Trojan-Banker category was the prevalent mobile malware threat with a 31.63% share of all detected malicious apps. Over 378,000 malicious installation packages were detected, including 119,688 mobile banking Trojan packages. Quarterly highlights In July, we discovered a malicious app targeting Brazilian users that may have used AI to automate fraud. The app was disguised as Google Play Protect, a suite of security services for Android devices. Malicious app imitating Google Play Protect The app’s code used the DistilBERT model to interpret natural-language commands sent from the C2 server. Traces left in the code suggest the server-side commands may also have been generated by a large language model (LLM). In August, we discovered a Trojan that analyzed images saved in the device’s gallery and took screenshots to look for banking data, including CVV codes. The malware used an on-device AI model to classify images. The app could also update this model, which gave the scammers a way to expand the Trojan’s functionality. In the third quarter, the infamous subscription Trojan detected as Trojan.AndroidOS.Subscriber.bh made it into Google Play again. This time, it was disguised as an app for creating keyboard themes. Subscription Trojan disguised as a keyboard theme app The Trojan opened a subscription link in a hidden WebView and intercepted the message containing the confirmation code. According to our data, the scammers mainly targeted users in Thailand. There were also new attacks on iOS users. In August, researchers at Socket discovered 13 infected PHP packages in the Packagist repository. The malicious payload injected links to fraudulent casinos into sites that used these packages and, on iOS devices only, a hidden iframe that loaded the DarkSword exploit kit. The attack delivered a spyware module that stole keychain contents, Wi-Fi passwords, SMS messages, photos, and other personal data. Other modules found in this campaign were used to steal crypto wallet data and the seed phrases used to recover them. SlowMist researchers found the same DarkSword exploit chain used in a fake app, FomoPeek. FomoPeek was published in the App Store, presenting itself as a crypto wallet tracker. The malware was designed to steal data from notes and crypto wallet apps. Also in August, we discovered infected versions of popular iOS apps distributed through Telegram (link in Russian). To install such an app, the attackers asked users to buy a developer certificate. The modified versions contained a malicious module that collected device information, took screenshots, and sent this data to a server. Mobile threat statistics The downward trend in attacks on mobile devices involving malware, adware, or unwanted software continued: the number fell to 1,668,368 in Q3 from 1,996,823 in Q2. Attacks on users of Kaspersky mobile solutions, Q1 2025 – Q3 2026 ( download ) In the third quarter, this decline was driven in part by fewer adware attacks, which we examine in more detail below. The number of Android malware samples grew compared to the previous reporting period, reaching 378,456. Detected malicious and potentially unwanted installation packages, Q3 2025 – Q3 2026 ( download ) The distribution of detected installation packages by type was as follows: Detected mobile apps by type, Q2*–Q3 2026 ( download ) * Data for the previous quarter may differ slightly from previously published data due to certain verdicts being retrospectively revised. The sharp rise in Trojan-Dropper apps comes from more droppers delivering known banking Trojans such as Mamont and Creduz. In the previous quarter, we described the trend of attackers “packaging” banking Trojans. The resulting malware is classified as droppers, which explains the growth. Note that standalone banking Trojans still rank first. Together with droppers, they account for more than half of all detected malicious apps. Share* of users attacked by the given type of malicious or potentially unwanted apps out of all targeted users of Kaspersky mobile products, Q2–Q3 2026 ( download ) * The total percentage may exceed 100% if the same users encountered multiple attack types. The number of AdWare.AndroidOS.HiddenAd and AdWare.AndroidOS.MobiDash attacks continued to decline, although adware traditionally ranks first by the number of attacked users. The growing share of Trojan-Dropper correlates with the increase in packaged banking Trojans described in the previous section. Among Trojan-Spy attacks, the biggest growth came from the BTMOB and SpyNote RAT Trojans, which are used to steal money. The main newcomer among Q3’s most widespread malware was the Trojan-Proxy.AndroidOS.Vo1d.b apps, delivered by preinstalled Trojans. These apps turn the device into an exit node of a VPN service. These attacks are dangerous for two reasons. First, they burn through internet traffic, which the user may be paying for, to relay other people’s data. Second, cybercriminals can use the infected device to attack online services and visit banned websites, breaking the law in the victim’s name.
